Data-source overview:
The appendix of a security-game paper provides the full mathematical model and proofs (Lemmas 1–2, Theorem 3) for repeated Stackelberg security games with two targets and two attacker types. It shows that committing to one of two extremal mixed strategies (m min or m max) forms a Perfect Bayesian Nash Equilibrium, prevents information leakage, and maximises the defender’s expected utility.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[67]

Inference-strategy justification:
The source is almost entirely formal proof text; no explicit “interventions” are written. Using moderate inference (edge-confidence 2) I translated the formal equilibrium prescription into a concrete deployable intervention: “compute and deploy the extremal mixed coverage strategy each round.” All other nodes map directly to distinct claims or mechanisms stated in the proofs.

Extraction-completeness explanation:
The fabric captures every causal chain present:  
Risk (defender loss) → Problem (information leakage) → Theoretical insight (attacker indifference blocks belief-updates) → Design rationale (choose extremal strategies) → Implementation mechanisms (linear programmes + backward induction) → Validation evidence (Lemma 1 & Theorem 3 proofs) → Intervention (deploy extremal strategy).  
All lemma/theorem results that justify the solution are represented, and no isolated nodes remain.

Key limitations:
• Proofs assume only two targets and two attacker types; applicability to larger games is not captured.  
• Intervention maturity is low because no empirical deployment data appear.  
• Edge confidence is generally 3 (medium) since evidence is purely theoretical rather than empirical.

Suggestions to improve the instruction set:
Clarify whether purely theoretical prescriptions (like equilibrium strategies) should be treated as “interventions” even when no implementation details beyond mathematical formulation are given; this affects lifecycle and maturity labelling.
